title: AI and Cultivated Meat. Near-Term Impacts of AI on the Commercial Viability of Cultivated Meat
authors: Hannah Moulange; William McAuliffe
type: original interview-based research and literature synthesis
access: full report text inspected
finding: Examines technical, economic, regulatory, consumer and capital constraints; separates demonstrated AI applications from prospective ones.
limitations: Five interviews and a non-systematic search do not represent the whole industry; proprietary applications may be invisible.
implication: Extend its bottleneck analysis with conditional policy decisions and measurable displacement tests rather than repeating an AI opportunity list.
funding: Rethink Priorities is a nonprofit with an animal-welfare research mission; specific report funding not confirmed here.

title: National Action Plan Germany
authors: Liliia Lisina; Pia Voltz
type: original stakeholder consultation and policy report
access: 17-page PDF inspected, especially PDF pp. 2, 4, 13-15
finding: Identifies four action areas: authorization support, scale-up finance, agricultural integration, and public trust. Reports 15 questionnaire responses and 10 interviews; seven interviewees came through the questionnaire.
limitations: Purposive ecosystem consultation; responses and interviews overlap and are not 25 independent respondents. Recommendations are not an adopted German government plan.
implication: Use as the initial policy-instrument inventory, then test when each instrument helps under alternative AI and displacement assumptions.
funding: EU Horizon Europe FEASTS, grant 101136749; CellAg has a sector-development mission. Cover lists Lisina and Voltz as authors; acknowledgments also credit Fabian Baumann with preparation.

title: Using Foresight for Food Systems Transformation A guide for policy makers practitioners and researchers
authors: Jim Woodhill; Bram Peters; Just Dengerink; Nicole De Paula; Rathana Peou Norbert Munns; Ludovica Nesbitt
access: PDF inspected; current linked file states Version 1.1 October 2025
finding: Organizes work around scoping, systems mapping, exploring futures and mobilizing change; includes power, participation and locally situated food systems.
limitations: A participatory process does not establish calibrated probabilities or causal policy effectiveness.
implication: Use the food-system framing, while attaching explicit evidence and review triggers to policy choices.
funding: Produced by Foresight4Food and UN Food Systems Coordination Hub. Acknowledgments identify support from the Netherlands through IFAD and Germany through the Hub Youth Leadership Programme; current PDF hosted by FAO.

title: Dynamic adaptive policy pathways A method for crafting robust decisions for a deeply uncertain world
authors: Marjolijn Haasnoot; Jan H. Kwakkel; Warren E. Walker; Judith ter Maat
type: peer-reviewed original method with worked case
access: full paper inspected, Global Environmental Change 23:485-498
finding: Combines action sequences with conditions under which an existing policy ceases to meet its objectives; illustrates the method in Rhine Delta water management.
limitations: Its food-system application is an adaptation proposed here, not a result established by the paper.
implication: Specify what to do now, what evidence to monitor and when to change an allocation.
funding: Affiliations are universities and Deltares; detailed grant disclosure not extracted.

title: OECD FAO Agricultural Outlook 2026–2035 Chapter 5 Meat
authors: OECD; Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
access: full chapter text inspected
finding: Projects continued global meat-market growth and describes productivity, prices, demographics and trade as drivers. It explicitly discusses AI use in livestock management.
limitations: A conditional baseline projection, not an observed future or a no-AI counterfactual. Its treatment of alternative proteins must be checked before subtracting another forecast.
implication: Use a dated conventional-market baseline and distinguish lower-than-baseline production from an absolute decline.
funding: Official intergovernmental publication.

title: How innovation-friendly is the EU Novel Food Regulation? The case of cellular agriculture
authors: Tilman Reinhardt; Alessandro Monaco
type: peer-reviewed original legal and empirical analysis
access: institutional abstract and bibliographic record inspected; full journal text not obtained
finding: Triangulates legal analysis with stakeholder evidence to examine effects of the Novel Food framework on cellular-agriculture innovation.
limitations: Abstract-only extraction; no specific delay estimate or survey effect size accepted into the report.
implication: Separate safety assessment, applicant capability and market-formation concerns.
funding: Institutional record identifies Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft project financing.

title: Animal Product Impact Scales 2026 Updated U.S. Estimates And The U.K.’s First Animal Product Impact Data
authors: Faunalytics; update led by Chris Bryant at Bryant Research
access: full explanation inspected; linked raw OSF files not retrieved
finding: Distinguishes animal lives and days of suffering by product and reporting unit; the 2026 update changes data and accounting assumptions.
limitations: The explanatory page is insufficient to audit every factor. Average product impacts and marginal production responses must not be conflated or counted twice.
implication: Audit the underlying factor definitions before translating procurement changes into animal outcomes.
funding: Animal-advocacy research organization; commissioning and modeling assumptions should accompany use.

title: Behavioral and neurophysiological evidence suggests affective pain experience in octopus
authors: Robyn J. Crook
access: publisher text and study highlights inspected; publisher retrieval intermittently unavailable
finding: Place-avoidance and relief-related behavior, together with neural evidence, support an affective-pain interpretation in octopuses.
limitations: Species- and experiment-specific evidence; it does not establish a universal welfare weight or identical sentience across all food animals.
implication: Animal outcomes should be explicit rather than inferred from a carbon-only objective.
funding: Funding not extracted; inspect full acknowledgments before publication.

title: Optimising Cheese Analogues Formulation using AI Applications
authors: Deneille Guiseppi; Rohun Tripathi
access: gallery project page inspected; linked Overleaf paper could not be fetched by web tool
finding: Describes a proof of concept combining computer vision and Bayesian optimization for cheese-analogue stretchability.
limitations: The gallery account does not establish a commercial cost reduction, improved nutrition or dairy displacement.
implication: Use as a worked handoff from technical performance to questions about validation, industrial relevance and adoption.
funding: Participant-produced description in the Sentient Futures project gallery.

title: Effective Advocacy Project
authors: Hubert Thieriot; Thomas Manandhar-Richardson
access: gallery page inspected; linked project site unavailable in web retrieval
finding: Maps arguments and actors in policy debates, illustrated through alternative proteins in Europe.
limitations: An actor map does not itself measure policy influence or intervention effectiveness.
implication: Build a small instrument-and-actor table rather than duplicate a broad influence map.
funding: Participant-produced project account.

title: Ideosphere
authors: Rei Nova; Mariana Oka; Niki Dupuis
access: gallery page inspected
finding: Describes AI baseline forecasts and human forecasting participation on welfare and AI questions.
limitations: A platform description does not demonstrate calibration or domain-specific forecast accuracy.
implication: A possible future benchmark venue; record performance before using its outputs as evidence.
funding: Participant-produced description.

title: CellAg Deutschland project overview
authors: CellAg Deutschland
access: organization page inspected
finding: Lists the FEASTS country contribution and identifies AltProtein.Jobs as part of CellAg since 2025.
limitations: This does not establish individual mentors' data permissions or access to hiring outcomes.
implication: Frame a precise data-feasibility request; do not assume access to private hiring records.
funding: CellAg is a sector-development nonprofit; promotional claims are not treated as independent evidence.

title: Scale-up economics for cultured meat
authors: David Humbird
access: full text via Wiley HTML
finding: The analysis argues that animal-cell culture faces hard scale limits from slow growth, metabolic inefficiency, catabolite inhibition, shear sensitivity, sterility costs, and expensive amino-acid/growth-factor media. It concludes that low-cost plant hydrolysate media and large metabolic efficiency gains are necessary but still insufficient for broad meat displacement.
limitations: Conceptual facilities; relies heavily on CHO/biopharma analogies because public cultivated-meat production data were scarce; unstructured cell mass rather than mature consumer products.
implication: Cultivated meat forecasts should require public milestone evidence for media cost, cell density, contamination control, and bioreactor productivity before assuming commodity displacement.
funding: Funding/conflict statement not found in inspected page section; author affiliation is DWH Process Consulting.

title: Environmental Impacts of Cultured Meat: A Cradle-to-Gate Life Cycle Assessment
authors: Derrick Risner; Patrick Negulescu; Yoonbin Kim; Cuong Nguyen; Justin B. Siegel; Edward S. Spang
type: cradle-to-gate life-cycle assessment with scenario analysis
access: full text/abstract via ACS, PubMed, and PMC landing pages
finding: Modeled near-term animal cell-based meat can have much higher environmental impacts than beef if production depends on highly refined growth media. The result turns on media processing assumptions and shows that environmental benefits require sustainable, low-refinement media and high-density proliferation.
limitations: Modeled LCA grounded in TEAs and engineering/database assumptions, not measurement from an operating commercial or pilot ACBM facility; near-term scenario, not an optimized mature industry; cradle-to-gate only; sensitive to media purification factor and TEA inputs.
implication: Public funding should treat growth-media supply chains as an environmental gating variable, not a technical detail; LCA claims should publish media assumptions.
funding: Inspected PubMed/PMC landing pages did not expose a conflict statement; affiliations include USDA AI Institute for Next Generation Food Systems.

title: Ex-ante life cycle assessment of commercial-scale cultivated meat production in 2030
authors: Pelle Sinke; Elliot Swartz; Hermes Sanctorum; Coen van der Giesen; Ingrid Odegard
access: publisher page and abstract/snippet via Springer
finding: The study projects that commercial-scale cultivated meat in 2030 could beat beef and pork on climate impacts when production and key supply chains use renewable energy, while global-average energy can leave it above pork and chicken. Medium efficiency, energy source, and supply-chain development are central.
limitations: Ex-ante 2030 scenario; relies on forward-looking assumptions and often private/primary inputs; corrected in 2023.
implication: Cultivated meat needs clean energy and verified medium efficiency to be climate-positive; policy should pair R&D with energy and transparent LCA standards.
funding: Funded by GAIA, The Good Food Institute, and CE Delft. Conflict statement: Elliot Swartz works at GFI; Hermes Sanctorum works as a private consultant for GAIA; Pelle Sinke, Ingrid Odegard, and Coen van der Giesen work at CE Delft.

title: Environmental Impacts of Cultured Meat Production
authors: Hanna L. Tuomisto; M. Joost Teixeira de Mattos
access: publisher abstract page via ACS
finding: This early LCA estimated large land, water, and GHG advantages over conventional European meat, assuming cyanobacteria hydrolysate as nutrient and energy source. It reported 78-96% lower GHGs, 99% lower land use, and 82-96% lower water use versus several conventional meats.
limitations: Highly speculative process assumptions; predates later TEA critiques and detailed media supply-chain concerns; energy use not uniformly lower than poultry.
implication: Optimistic LCAs are useful as possibility proofs but should not anchor forecasts unless their nutrient, energy, and scale assumptions are still credible.
funding: Funding/conflict statement not found in inspected abstract page.

title: Anticipatory Life Cycle Analysis of In Vitro Biomass Cultivation for Cultured Meat Production in the United States
authors: Carolyn S. Mattick; Amy E. Landis; Braden R. Allenby; Nicholas J. Genovese
access: publisher metadata/abstract via ASU and ACS-reference snippets
finding: This study compared a future in vitro biomass system with beef, pork, poultry, and prior cultured-meat estimates, emphasizing that cultured meat may trade agricultural land and methane reductions for industrial energy demand. It helped establish the counterpoint to early very optimistic LCAs.
limitations: Anticipatory model with uncertain future technology; U.S. framing; not based on commercial cultivated-meat plant data.
implication: Forecasts should compare land-use benefits against industrial energy intensity, especially under non-decarbonized grids.
funding: Funding/conflict statement not found in inspected pages.

title: Simple and effective serum-free medium for sustained expansion of bovine satellite cells for cell cultured meat
authors: Andrew J. Stout; Addison B. Mirliani; Miriam L. Rittenberg; Michelle Shub; Eugene C. White; John S. K. Yuen Jr.; David L. Kaplan
access: full publisher abstract and PubMed/PMC landing pages
finding: The study adapted a low-cost serum-free B8 medium into Beefy-9 by adding recombinant albumin. It supported bovine satellite-cell expansion over seven passages with average doubling time around 39 hours while preserving myogenicity, reducing dependence on fetal bovine serum.
limitations: Lab-scale bovine satellite cells; not proof of food-grade commodity media, suspension production, or large bioreactor economics.
implication: Serum-free media progress is real but should be funded with scale, food-grade inputs, cost accounting, and species/cell-type reproducibility as explicit endpoints.
funding: Crossmark reports NIH funding P41EB002520 and no competing interests.

title: Spontaneous immortalization of chicken fibroblasts generates stable, high-yield cell lines for serum-free production of cultured meat
authors: L. Pasitka; M. Cohen; A. Ehrlich; B. Gildor; E. Reuveni; M. Ayyash; G. Wissotsky; A. Herscovici; R. Kaminker; A. Niv; R. Bitcover; O. Dadia; A. Rudik; A. Voloschin; M. Shimoni; Y. Cinnamon; Y. Nahmias
access: metadata and conflict statement via Crossref; publisher page referenced by RP
finding: The study demonstrates spontaneously immortalized chicken fibroblast lines intended for stable, high-yield, serum-free cultivated-meat production. It is evidence that relevant cell-line engineering can improve growth and production traits, especially for poultry.
limitations: Company-linked work; chicken fibroblasts only; does not by itself establish low-cost, large-scale commodity production or consumer displacement.
implication: Cell-line banks and transparent performance benchmarks can reduce duplicative private R&D and make AI-assisted optimization more effective.
funding: Several authors were employees, consultants, directors, or shareholders of Believer Meats; Y. Nahmias was CSO/director/shareholder.

title: Multi-objective Bayesian algorithm automatically discovers low-cost high-growth serum-free media for cellular agriculture application
authors: Zachary Cosenza; David E. Block; Keith Baar; Xingyu Chen
access: full text via Wiley HTML
finding: A multi-information-source Bayesian optimization workflow explored serum-free media for C2C12 muscle cells, balancing growth and cost. It found media with more than 100% greater growth than control and another with 23% higher growth at 62.5% of control cost from limited experiments.
limitations: Mouse C2C12 cells, adapted line, short lab campaign; serum-free does not automatically mean animal-component-free, and methods describe Matrigel use during adaptation before dilution cloning selected cells that survived without it; not food-relevant bovine/chicken suspension production; media cost coefficients are not final commodity costs.
implication: AI can materially improve experimental search when paired with wet-lab data; open media datasets may be a high-leverage public good.
funding: Article page says authors had nothing to report in acknowledgments and no conflicts to disclose; data openly available on GitHub.

title: Toward sustainable culture media: Using artificial intelligence to optimize reduced-serum formulations for cultivated meat
authors: Amin Nikkhah; Abbas Rohani; Mohammad Zarei; Ajay Kulkarni; Feras A. Batarseh; Nicole Tichenor Blackstone; Reza Ovissipour
access: PubMed abstract and conflict statement
finding: The study used RSM, radial-basis-function neural networks, and a genetic algorithm to optimize reduced-serum media for a zebrafish cultivated-meat cell line across growth rate, global warming potential, and cost. The model reported high predictive efficiency for the selected outputs; this is predictive optimization, not evidence of causal production-scale effects.
limitations: Zebrafish line and reduced-serum formulation; model-driven optimization is not yet proof of animal-free, food-scale media or market readiness.
implication: AI should be directed toward multi-objective optimization that includes environment and cost, not just growth; actual serum-free and animal-component-free validation remain separate milestones.
funding: PubMed lists declaration of no conflict of interest.

title: Projected environmental benefits of replacing beef with microbial protein
authors: Florian Humpenöder; Benjamin Leon Bodirsky; Isabelle Weindl; Hermann Lotze-Campen; Tomas Linder; Alexander Popp
access: publisher page and PubMed abstract
finding: Using the MAgPIE land-use model, the study projected that replacing 20% of per-capita ruminant meat protein with microbial protein by 2050 could offset future pasture expansion and cut annual deforestation and related CO2 emissions roughly in half, with nonlinear saturation at higher replacement levels.
limitations: Assumes consumer acceptance and microbial-protein supply; does not fully resolve product taste, price, nutrition, or electricity impacts of production.
implication: Partial ruminant-meat displacement through fermentation can yield large land-use gains; target beef first rather than assuming uniform substitution across meats.
funding: Publisher page lists EU Horizon 2020, University of Tokyo, Research Council of Norway, Wellcome Trust, Rockefeller Foundation, and IKEA Foundation support; authors declare no competing interests.

title: A life cycle environmental sustainability analysis of microbial protein production via power-to-food approaches
authors: J. Sillman; V. Uusitalo; V. Ruuskanen; L. Ojala; H. Kahiluoto; R. Soukka; J. Ahola
access: full text via Springer HTML
finding: The LCA finds that microbial protein from power-to-food systems can have much lower land occupation, eutrophication, and blue-water impacts than soybean and other proteins in best-case setups. Electricity source and electricity-to-biomass efficiency dominate environmental performance; some configurations perform worse.
limitations: Theoretical/early technology; commercial feasibility, food safety, and large reactors still unresolved; construction and some minor flows excluded.
implication: Microbial protein is attractive under abundant clean electricity and efficient bioreactors; energy-system planning and TEA should be integrated with food policy.
funding: Funding/conflict statement not found in inspected output; open-access publisher page inspected.

title: Life cycle assessment of burger patties produced with extruded meat substitutes
authors: Wiebe Saerens; Sergiy Smetana; Leen Van Campenhout; Volker Lammers; Volker Heinz
type: cradle-to-gate life-cycle assessment with production-scale extrusion data
access: ScienceDirect abstract/snippet
finding: The study compared high-moisture and low-moisture extruded soy and pumpkin-seed plant burger patties with beef, pork, and chicken patties. Plant-based patties had at least tenfold lower environmental impact than meat patties; high-moisture extrusion generally outperformed TVP by 20-40%.
limitations: Cradle-to-gate and ready-to-pack patties; packaging/distribution assumed similar; functional-unit and ingredient choices affect comparisons.
implication: Plant-based analogues already have stronger environmental evidence than cultivated meat; improving texture, nutrition, and adoption may be more near-term than solving cell-culture scale.
funding: Funding/conflict statement not found in inspected abstract/snippet.

title: A randomized crossover trial on the effect of plant-based compared with animal-based meat on trimethylamine-N-oxide and cardiovascular disease risk factors in generally healthy adults: Study With Appetizing Plantfood-Meat Eating Alternative Trial (SWAP-MEAT)
authors: Anthony Crimarco; Sparkle Springfield; Christina Petlura; Taylor Streaty; Kristen Cunanan; Justin Lee; Priya Fielding-Singh; Matthew M. Carter; Madeline A. Topf; Hannah C. Wastyk; Erica D. Sonnenburg; Justin L. Sonnenburg; Christopher D. Gardner
access: Crossref metadata and NCBI/PubMed XML abstract
finding: Thirty-six generally healthy adults consumed at least two servings per day of plant-based meat alternatives and animal meat for eight weeks each, with no washout. Plant phases had lower overall TMAO, LDL cholesterol, and body weight, though TMAO showed an order effect.
limitations: Small, short, single-site trial using specific commercial-style plant-based products; no washout; does not generalize to all plant proteins, fermentation biomass, cultivated meat, or whole-food diets.
implication: Plant-based meat can be compatible with improved cardiovascular risk markers in some contexts, but policy claims should stay product-specific and should track sodium, processing, and nutritional quality.
funding: Crossref lists Beyond Meat Inc., NIH/NHLBI, Stanford Clinical and Translational Science, and NIH UL1 TR001085 funding. Products studied were plant-based alternative meats, not all plant proteins.

title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold
authors: John Jumper; Richard Evans; Alexander Pritzel; Tim Green; Michael Figurnov; Olaf Ronneberger; Kathryn Tunyasuvunakool; Russ Bates; Augustin Zidek; Anna Potapenko; Alex Bridgland; Clemens Meyer; Simon A. A. Kohl; Andrew J. Ballard; Andrew Cowie; Bernardino Romera-Paredes; Stanislav Nikolov; Rishub Jain; Jonas Adler; Trevor Back; Stig Petersen; David Reiman; Ellen Clancy; Michal Zielinski; Martin Steinegger; Michalina Pacholska; Tamas Berghammer; Sebastian Bodenstein; David Silver; Oriol Vinyals; Andrew W. Senior; Koray Kavukcuoglu; Pushmeet Kohli; Demis Hassabis
access: Nature/PubMed abstract and ethics declaration
finding: AlphaFold dramatically improves protein-structure prediction from sequence, reducing a major bottleneck in biological hypothesis generation and protein engineering. For alternative proteins, it is upstream infrastructure for enzyme, growth factor, and protein-design work, not evidence of commercial food displacement.
limitations: Structure prediction is not expression yield, food texture, process economics, regulation, or consumer adoption; not an alternative-protein commercialization study.
implication: AI protein tools can accelerate input discovery, but forecasts should not translate structural accuracy directly into food-market impact.
funding: Several DeepMind authors filed patent applications related to ML protein-structure prediction; other authors declared no competing interests.

title: Precision Dairy Farming, Robotic Milking, and Profitability in the United States
authors: Jonathan McFadden; Zach Raff
type: USDA ERS empirical economic report using farm survey data
access: USDA ERS report page and summary
finding: USDA ERS reports that robotic milking, or use of two or more precision technologies, is estimated to raise U.S. dairy net returns by about 13% on average after accounting for farm and operator characteristics. Technologies include sensors, data analytics, automation, milking, breeding, and cow-level management tools.
limitations: Profitability association/estimation in dairy; not all tools are modern AI; does not directly estimate emissions or animal-welfare displacement effects.
implication: AI and automation can strengthen incumbent animal agriculture by improving margins; alternative-protein forecasts must model this competitive response.
funding: USDA Economic Research Service publication; no private conflict statement noted on inspected page.

title: A machine learning framework to predict the next month's daily milk yield, milk composition and milking frequency for cows in a robotic dairy farm
authors: Boyu Ji; Thomas Banhazi; Clive J. C. Phillips; Chaoyuan Wang; Baoming Li
type: machine-learning prediction study using robotic dairy farm data
access: ScienceDirect abstract/snippet and Crossref metadata
finding: The study trained ML models on five years of behavior, health, productivity, and milk-quality data from 80 cows in a robotic dairy farm to forecast the next 28 days of milk yield, composition, and milking frequency. Reported prediction accuracy exceeded 80%, with R2 above 0.90.
limitations: Single robotic dairy context; predictive management tool rather than direct proof of lower cost, lower emissions, or welfare gains; broader validation needed.
implication: Incumbent livestock systems are data-rich and can also benefit from AI; alternative proteins need advantages that survive smart-farm productivity improvements.
funding: Crossref lists University of Southern Queensland award 17REA007; conflict statement not captured in inspected metadata.

title: Most plant-based meat alternative buyers also buy meat: an analysis of household demographics, habit formation, and buying behavior among meat alternative buyers
authors: Zachary T. Neuhofer; Jayson L. Lusk
access: open access full text
finding: About 20% of households bought a plant-based meat alternative at least once, but only 12% bought more than once. Only 2.79% of households purchased plant-based meat alternatives without buying ground meat in the studied ground-meat/PBMA categories. 86% of plant-based meat alternative buyers also bought ground meat. After a household's first plant-based meat alternative purchase, ground meat consumption did not fall.
limitations: Covers ground/patty-like products and ground-meat co-purchasing rather than all meat or all alternative proteins. The panel period ends in 2020 and may not capture later price, quality, and availability changes. Household purchases do not prove consumption or food waste effects.
implication: Policy should measure net displacement using scanner, foodservice, and production data rather than treating alternative-protein sales as one-for-one animal-product reductions.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: transaction-level household scanner panel aggregated weekly for 38,966 households
geography: United States households in IRI scanner data, November 2018-November 2020
bibliographic_note: Neuhofer, Zachary T., and Jayson L. Lusk. 2022. Scientific Reports 12, Article 13062.

title: Impact of plant-based meat alternatives on cattle inventories and greenhouse gas emissions
authors: Jayson L. Lusk; Dan Blaustein-Rejto; Saloni Shah; Glynn T. Tonsor
access: open access full text
finding: A 10% plant-based meat price decline or demand increase was estimated to reduce U.S. cattle production by about 0.15%. The same shock was estimated to increase plant-based meat consumption substantially but produce small cattle-inventory effects. Producer welfare losses and consumer welfare gains were material but modest relative to market size. Global emissions reductions depended on trade and land-use assumptions.
limitations: Model outputs are sensitive to cross-price elasticities, cattle supply elasticity, and the share of cattle value attributable to ground beef. It models U.S. cattle impacts rather than poultry, pork, eggs, dairy, fish, or multispecies animal welfare. It does not prove future consumer preferences under improved products.
implication: Price parity is useful but insufficient; displacement policy needs target categories, market-share thresholds, elasticities, and production endpoints.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: calibrated economic model using demand elasticities, cattle supply, beef trade, land-use and emissions parameters
geography: United States beef and plant-based meat markets, with global trade effects
bibliographic_note: Lusk, Jayson L., Dan Blaustein-Rejto, Saloni Shah, and Glynn T. Tonsor. 2022. Environmental Research Letters 17(2):024035.

title: Estimating plant-based milk impacts on U.S. fluid milk prices and quantities
authors: Sangwon Lee; Daniel A. Sumner
access: ScienceDirect article page; search-accessible full abstract and methods text indicated open/CC status
finding: Plant-based milk was closer to organic and lactose-free cow's milk than to conventional cow's milk. Counterfactual removal of plant-based milk would raise organic, lactose-free, and conventional cow's milk quantities. The authors estimate that each gallon of plant-based milk displaced 0.68 gallons of cow's milk in the data. Plant-based milk was not found to be the primary driver of the long-run decline in U.S. fluid cow's milk.
limitations: The displacement ratio comes from a static counterfactual and should not be read as a causal long-run ratio. The model treats shopping occasions as single-choice events and does not fully model bundles, stockpiling, or habit formation. Dairy displacement may not generalize to meat categories.
implication: Category-specific displacement estimates matter; dairy alternatives may produce measurable replacement before meat analogues do.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: random-coefficients discrete-choice model over household shopping occasions
geography: United States NielsenIQ household panel and store scanner data, 2018-2020
bibliographic_note: Lee, Sangwon, and Daniel A. Sumner. 2026. Food Policy 142:103119.

title: Price of change: Does a small alteration to the price of meat and vegetarian options affect their sales?
authors: Emma E. Garnett; Andrew Balmford; Theresa M. Marteau; Mark A. Pilling; Chris Sandbrook
access: publisher open access; Cambridge accepted version and data available
finding: Vegetarian meals were made GBP0.20 cheaper and meat meals GBP0.20 more expensive. Vegetarian sales increased by 3.2 percentage points overall. Meat sales did not significantly change overall, while fish sales declined. The largest response came from diners already most likely to choose vegetarian or vegan meals.
limitations: Single college setting limits generalizability. Small price changes may be less salient when diners pay by university card. The intervention affected meal choice, not upstream animal production.
implication: Procurement and pricing should be tested in real purchase settings and segmented by baseline diet; price parity is not automatically mass substitution.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: nine-week field experiment over 106 mealtimes and 13,840 hot meal selections
geography: University of Cambridge college cafeteria diners, United Kingdom
bibliographic_note: Garnett, Emma E., Andrew Balmford, Theresa M. Marteau, Mark A. Pilling, and Chris Sandbrook. 2021. Journal of Environmental Psychology 75:101589.

title: Can you default to vegan? Plant-based defaults to change dining practices on college campuses
authors: Joel Ginn; Gregg Sparkman
access: publisher abstract and methods visible; data and supplemental information reported at OSF
finding: The vegan default increased vegan dishes served at intervention stations by about 58.3%. The intervention reduced meat consumption at targeted stations by an estimated 21.4-57.2%. Total servings from the station declined by 26.1%, smaller than the meat decline. The study measured served dishes rather than survey intentions.
limitations: Campus dining stations are not representative of all foodservice or retail contexts. Some reduction may reflect diners selecting elsewhere rather than full replacement. The result is site-level consumption change, not direct production displacement.
implication: Public institutions can run low-cost randomized procurement and menu-default trials with actual servings, waste, satisfaction, and repeat-purchase outcomes.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: three-month field experiment with station-days randomized to plant-based default or no-default control
geography: Campus cafeterias across three U.S. universities
bibliographic_note: Ginn, Joel, and Gregg Sparkman. 2024. Journal of Environmental Psychology 93:102226.

title: Estimating global numbers of farmed fishes killed for food annually from 1990 to 2019
authors: Alison Mood; Elena Lara; Natasha K. Boyland; Phil Brooke
access: open access full text via Cambridge/PMC
finding: The study estimates 78-171 billion farmed finfishes killed for food in 2019, midpoint 124 billion. The midpoint exceeded combined farmed birds and mammals slaughtered that year. The largest numbers were concentrated in Asian aquaculture and small-bodied species. The paper recommends FAO publish fish counts alongside tonnage.
limitations: FAO aquaculture statistics are themselves estimates and may under- or over-report in some settings. Mean-weight estimates vary by species, country, and production system. The estimates cover finfish and exclude many invertebrates.
implication: Animal-impact policy should include species- and individual-count endpoints, not only kilograms, protein, or CO2-equivalent.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: species/category-level conversion of production tonnage into estimated individual fish counts
bibliographic_note: Mood, Alison, Elena Lara, Natasha K. Boyland, and Phil Brooke. 2023. Animal Welfare 32:e12.

title: FDA Completes First Pre-Market Consultation for Human Food Made Using Animal Cell Culture Technology
authors: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
access: official full text
finding: FDA stated it had no further questions at that time about UPSIDE Foods' safety conclusion. The consultation evaluated production process, cultured cell material, cell lines and banks, manufacturing controls, and inputs. FDA emphasized that the voluntary consultation is not an approval process. The product still needed to meet other federal requirements before market entry.
limitations: A no-further-questions letter is not broad approval of all cultivated products. It does not resolve labeling, USDA inspection, price, scale, consumer adoption, or animal displacement. The communication covers one company/product consultation.
implication: Policy investments should fund transparent safety dossier capacity, regulator staffing, and post-market monitoring before assuming cultivated meat can scale responsibly.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
geography: United States; UPSIDE Foods cultured chicken consultation
bibliographic_note: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. 2022. Constituent Update.

title: Climate Action in SG (Dec 2020): Novel food as a sustainable food option
authors: Singapore Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment
access: official full text
finding: Singapore described itself as the first country to approve sale of lab-grown meat. The product was Eat Just cultured chicken bites under Singapore's novel food regulatory framework. The communication links novel food regulation with food resilience and agri-tech strategy.
limitations: Newsletter language is high-level and not a technical safety assessment. It does not provide market penetration or production displacement evidence. Singapore's import-dependent food strategy may not generalize to large livestock-producing countries.
implication: Regulatory sandboxes can accelerate learning, but fair global policy should distinguish food-security strategy from proof of animal-production displacement.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: government newsletter summarizing regulatory milestone and innovation agenda
geography: Singapore; Eat Just cultured chicken approval
bibliographic_note: Singapore Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment. 2020. Climate Action in SG newsletter.

title: Novel Food legislation: Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 and implementing acts
authors: European Commission, Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety
access: official full text and links to regulations
finding: Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 has applied since 1 January 2018. Novel food categories include foods from cell cultures and new production processes. Novel foods require pre-market authorization and EFSA safety evaluation when consulted. EU authorization uses a Union list and can include labeling, conditions of use, and specifications.
limitations: The page is procedural; it is not an impact assessment of alternative proteins. Authorization timelines and outcomes vary by dossier quality and member-state risk management. The framework does not itself fund market access, scale-up, or just-transition measures.
implication: Public investment should include dossier science, transparent labeling, nutrition evaluation, and regulator capacity so approval processes are credible rather than merely fast.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.

title: Food safety aspects of cell-based food
authors: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations; World Health Organization
access: official full text PDF
finding: The report identifies potential food safety hazards across cell sourcing, cell lines, media, scaffolds, bioprocessing, harvesting, and post-processing. It emphasizes that many hazards are not entirely new, but assessment must fit cell-based processes. The report is intended to help authorities, especially in low- and middle-income countries, prepare regulatory frameworks. It stresses terminology, labeling, stakeholder communication, and technical preparedness.
limitations: It is a safety and regulatory preparedness document, not proof of sustainability, price parity, or displacement. Commercial cell-based foods remain unavailable or limited in most markets. The evidence base is still developing and product-specific.
implication: A fair 10-20 year strategy should build public safety science and regulator capacity before products diffuse unevenly across jurisdictions.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: 145-page technical report based on literature review and FAO-led expert consultation
geography: Global regulators, with case studies including Singapore, Israel, and Qatar

title: Livestock sector development for poverty reduction: an economic and policy perspective - Livestock's many virtues
authors: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
access: official full text HTML and PDF
finding: FAO states that livestock contribute to the livelihoods of an estimated 70% of the world's rural poor. The report treats livestock as income, assets, risk management, nutrition, manure, traction, and social/cultural capital. It argues policy and institutions often fail to favor poor livestock keepers. It identifies conditions under which livestock can support poverty reduction.
limitations: The report predates the recent alternative-protein investment wave. It does not resolve environmental or animal-welfare tradeoffs. Livelihood roles differ sharply by species, region, gender, market access, and wealth.
implication: Fair alternative-protein policy should pair demand reduction in high-consumption settings with producer transition finance, local food-security analysis, and livelihood safeguards.

title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
authors: Danny Halawi; Fred Zhang; Chen Yueh-Han; Jacob Steinhardt
access: open access full text and public code repository
finding: The system neared the crowd aggregate of competitive forecasters and sometimes surpassed it in studied settings. The authors used questions published after model knowledge cutoffs to reduce leakage concerns. Retrieval and aggregation were central; this was not just a single unassisted model prompt. The work suggests scalable institutional forecasting assistance is plausible.
limitations: The system is engineered and benchmarked; performance may not transfer to ill-posed policy questions. Question quality, resolution criteria, retrieval sources, and time horizons strongly affect validity. The human comparator is a forecasting-platform crowd aggregate, not an identified superforecaster panel; reported standard errors are tied to the benchmark design and should not be generalized as robust policy-domain calibration. Near-human performance does not imply independence, causal understanding, or robust calibration in a new domain.
implication: Use LLMs for structured research, base rates, and probability elicitation only inside a scored forecasting protocol with human benchmarks.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: retrieval-augmented LM system with search, reasoning, probability generation, and aggregation
geography: Forecasting questions from competitive forecasting platforms, evaluated after model knowledge cutoffs
bibliographic_note: Halawi, Danny, Fred Zhang, Chen Yueh-Han, and Jacob Steinhardt. 2024. arXiv:2402.18563; NeurIPS 2024.

title: Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy
authors: Philipp Schoenegger; Indre Tuminauskaite; Peter S. Park; Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos; Philip E. Tetlock
access: open access full text via Science Advances/PMC
finding: The median LLM crowd beat a 50% no-information Brier baseline. The LLM crowd's mean Brier score was statistically indistinguishable from the human crowd in the studied question set. Most individual models showed poor calibration and an acquiescence-like bias. LLMs improved after seeing human crowd medians, but simple human-machine averaging outperformed their own updating.
limitations: Only 31 binary questions were used in the main ensemble comparison. The equivalence bounds were wide and calibration problems remained. The ensemble used accessible models and interfaces from a particular period; model behavior changes over time. Repeated model queries are aggregation inputs, not independent real-world events or proof of robust calibration.
implication: LLM ensembles can be useful if scored, calibrated, and compared to human and hybrid aggregates; they are not automatic proxy superforecasters.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: LLM ensemble forecasts compared with human crowd medians using Brier scores and calibration analysis
geography: 31 binary Metaculus tournament questions; 12 LLMs; 925 human forecasters
bibliographic_note: Schoenegger, Philipp, Indre Tuminauskaite, Peter S. Park, Rafael Valdece Sousa Bastos, and Philip E. Tetlock. 2024. Science Advances 10(45):eadp1528.

title: Diminished diversity-of-thought in a standard large language model
authors: Peter S. Park; Philipp Schoenegger; Chongyang Zhu
access: abstract via PubMed; full text available via PMC
finding: The study reports diminished diversity of thought in a standard LLM relative to human distributions. It provides a direct warning for ensemble claims: multiple samples from similar systems may not equal independent judgments. Lower diversity can reduce the error-cancellation benefits expected from crowd aggregation.
limitations: This is not an alternative-protein forecasting study. It does not score long-horizon policy forecasts directly. Model versions and prompting strategies can change measured diversity.
implication: Any AI-assisted forecasting protocol should measure pairwise error correlations, model-family diversity, and effective independent sample size.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
geography: Large language model outputs compared with human samples across judgment tasks
bibliographic_note: Park, Peter S., Philipp Schoenegger, and Chongyang Zhu. 2024. Behavior Research Methods 56(6):5754-5770.

title: Identifying and Cultivating Superforecasters as a Method of Improving Probabilistic Predictions
authors: Barbara A. Mellers; Eric Stone; Terry Murray; Angela Minster; Nick Rohrbaugh; Michael Bishop; Eva Chen; Joshua Baker; Yuan Hou; Michael C. Horowitz; Lyle Ungar; Philip E. Tetlock
access: publisher abstract and indexed metadata; full text may require subscription
finding: Superforecasters were partly selected and partly cultivated through training, teaming, tracking, motivation, and feedback. Top performers maintained unusually high accuracy across many questions and years. Performance depended on probabilistic reasoning, open-mindedness, updating, and enriched team environments. The result is a benchmark for disciplined human forecasting, not merely a crowd-size effect.
limitations: Geopolitical tournament results may not transfer automatically to food-system technology forecasts. Superforecaster performance required selection, feedback, and institutional design. The study predates modern LLM systems.
implication: Alternative-protein forecasts should be run as scored tournaments or prediction ledgers, not narrative scenario workshops alone.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
study_design: multi-year tournament analysis identifying top forecasters and team/selection/training effects
geography: U.S. Intelligence Community-sponsored geopolitical forecasting tournaments
bibliographic_note: Mellers, Barbara A., Eric Stone, Terry Murray, Angela Minster, Nick Rohrbaugh, Michael Bishop, Eva Chen, Joshua Baker, Yuan Hou, Michael C. Horowitz, Lyle Ungar, and Philip E. Tetlock. 2015. Perspectives on Psychological Science 10(3):267-281.

title: Annex II: Glossary - scenario, climate prediction, and climate projection definitions
authors: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
access: official full text
finding: A scenario is a plausible description of how the future may develop based on coherent assumptions. The glossary states that scenarios are neither predictions nor forecasts. A climate prediction or forecast estimates actual future evolution and is usually probabilistic. A projection is conditional on an emissions, concentration, land-use, or socioeconomic scenario.
limitations: Climate-assessment terminology is not a complete food-system forecasting method. Scenarios can still be misused if readers infer unstated likelihoods. The glossary does not specify how to score alternative-protein forecasts.
implication: Use scenarios to stress-test strategy and forecasts to allocate bets; do not claim a narrative pathway is likely unless it is probabilistically elicited and scored.
funding: Not extracted from inspected material; check acknowledgments before publication.
bibliographic_note: IPCC. 2022. Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, Annex II: Glossary.
